text: Write map, filter and reduce by hand, then compose them. Fill in the three blanks.
choices: static <T,R> List<R> map(List<T> in, Function<T,R> f) {
List<R> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (T x : in) ___; return out; }
static <T> List<T> filter(List<T> in, Predicate<T> p) {
List<T> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (T x : in) ___; return out; }
static <T> T reduce(List<T> in, T id, BinaryOperator<T> op) {
T acc = id; for (T x : in) ___; return acc; }
System.out.println(reduce(map(filter(ns, n -> n % 2 == 0), n -> n * n), 0, Integer::sum));
explanation: Verified: 220 — the sum of the squares of the evens from 1 to 10, matching the equivalent loop. Writing the three by hand is worth doing once, because it shows that the identity in `reduce` is not decoration: an empty input returns it, so it must be genuinely neutral. Choose 1 for a sum and every test with non-empty data still passes.
